Lost

A play in four acts, as performed on 23 November 2026

All the World a Play

Are Samantha and Joe alone in this forest, or has someone else been here, or is someone here still? What do these two make of this place, and of each other, once they know, or if they never find out?

The Players

Who is in it

Samantha

Hi, I’m Samantha. A hiker who woke up in a forest with no idea how I got here—yesterday’s just... gone, I guess? There’s a stranger standing nearby in a red shirt, and I don’t trust him yet. But we’re both lost, so maybe we figure it out together. Or maybe not. What happened to me?

Joe

Uh, hey. I’m Joe. I woke up in this forest with no idea how I got here—last night’s just... gone. There’s a woman nearby, a total stranger, and honestly I don’t know if she’s a friend or a problem. I need water, answers, a way out. But maybe... maybe this is what I’ve been waiting for?

Marta

Comes into the play in Chapter Nine.

Act One

Two Strangers in a Meadow

Chapter One

Breakfast off a Stranger’s Bush

The berries · Saturday, morning, 07:00

Samantha and Joe wake a few paces apart beside the laden berry bush at Berries3, throats dry and bellies empty, with no memory of how they came here and nobody else in sight.

❦

Samantha and Joe wake a few paces apart beside the laden berry bush at the berries, throats dry and bellies empty, with no memory of how they came here and nobody else in sight.

Joe and Samantha are now at the berries.

Samantha edges around the bush, keeping it between herself and the man, and picks a handful of berries. “Okay, so... I’m going to eat some of these. You stay over there. Fair?”

Joe “Fair. Totally fair. I’m Joe, by the way. And—okay, weird question, but do you have any idea how we got here? Because I’ve got nothing.”

Samantha “Joe. Right. I’m Samantha. And I’ve got about as much as you’ve got, so... don’t look at me for answers.”

Joe plucks a single berry from the bush and keeps it in his hand. “Samantha. Cool. Okay, so we’re both equally lost — that’s, uh, weirdly comforting? Are those berries safe, or are you the test subject?”

Samantha eats one berry from her handful, keeping her eyes on Joe. “Somebody’s gotta be the test subject, right? Watch me for a minute. If I stop talking, they’re poison. If I keep talking... well, you’re stuck with that either way.”

Joe “Deal. Though one berry’s kind of a small sample size. If you’re still talking in five minutes, I’m eating mine.”

Samantha takes a second berry from her handful and eats it. “Two berries down, still talking. See? Durable. So what’s your deal, Joe—do you actually hike, or did you just wander into the woods in chinos?”

Joe pops the berry into his mouth and eats it. “Okay, busted — I’m not a hiker. I built radios in my uncle’s garage every summer. Chinos were just what I woke up in. Your turn: you hike?”

Samantha “Uh, yeah, actually. Gear and everything—boots, pendleton, the whole thing. Which is kind of the creepy part: dressed for this, no memory of walking in.”

Joe “Okay, so somebody dressed us both. Grey pants, both of us — that’s a pattern, right? That’s not random.”

Samantha “Okay, fine, pattern. Then where’s the rest of it? No pack, no water bottle, nothing in my pockets. You got anything on you but chinos?”

Joe pats his pockets and turns them out, showing they’re empty. “Nope. No wallet, no keys, no phone. Whoever dressed us took everything — which, honestly, is kind of the creepiest part so far.”

Samantha “Unless the pattern’s backwards, right? I’m dressed for it, you’re not — maybe it just takes people wherever it finds them, dressed or not.”

Chapter Two

Which Way Is Water

The berries · Saturday, morning, 07:15

At the berry bush, Samantha is still on its far side with what is left of her handful, and Joe stays on his own side with his pockets hanging out empty. The berries have taken the edge off their hunger but not their thirst; Joe wants to set off at once the way he reckons water lies, and Samantha, who says she hikes, distrusts his hurry.

❦

Joe steps back from the bush, shades his eyes, and slowly turns, scanning the meadow grass and treeline. Joe makes a slow turn without picking out a clear sign. “Backwards pattern, sure. But water doesn’t care about patterns—it cares about slope. Gimme a second, I’m reading the land here.”

Samantha “Okay, radio boy—so what’s the land telling you? Because from here, everything looks like it slopes everywhere.”

Joe “Southeast, maybe. Grass is thicker that way—thicker usually means wetter soil. It’s a hunch, not gospel.”

Samantha “Thicker grass could just mean shade, though. I’d pick the steepest downhill and follow it—less guessing that way, I think.”

Joe “Fine, shade—sure. But which downhill, though? This meadow dips like three ways. Pick one, and I’ll go with it.”

Samantha “South, I think. There’s more birdsong over that dip—morning birds like hanging around water. But nobody’s sprinting off yet, okay? My throat’s still full of berry dust.”

Joe “Okay, no sprinting. And actually, the birdsong thing is—that’s basically data, I’ll give you that. So how long have you been hiking, anyway?”

Samantha “Since I was a kid, off and on. Enough to know you drink before you’re dying of it, not after. So—south, when we go. Not yet.”

Samantha crouches and lifts her fingers to feel the breeze on the back of her hand. “Air’s cooler coming up out of that southern dip—feel it? South it is, when we go. Trust the bird data.”

Joe “Cool air — that’s basically evaporation off water, that’s real data. Okay, south. Just… not too much later, yeah? My mouth’s already cardboard.”

Joe crouches, sweeps his hand through the meadow grass, and holds up his damp palm for Samantha to see. “Dew’s already burning off. Hour from now this meadow’s a frying pan. Southeast — wetter soil, I’d bet on it. Soon, okay?”

Samantha rises from the grass. “Joe — that’s just morning, not a direction. South, like we agreed. Give me two minutes, then we walk.”

Chapter Three

Somebody Else’s Boots

The spring · Saturday, morning, 07:33

After a few minutes walking south from the berry bush, Samantha and Joe, both parched, come on a spring of clear water. Pressed into the mud at its edge are fresh bootprints that neither of them made.

❦

Joe and Samantha walk to the spring (4 min).

Samantha kneels at the spring’s edge, sets down her berries, cups her hands to drink, then gathers the berries back into her wet hand. “Oh thank god, it’s actually clean—look how clear. Okay, don’t laugh at me, I’m doing this.”

Joe crouches by the bootprints at the spring’s edge and points at them. “Laugh? You just found drinking water, I could kiss this spring. Wait—no, look. Right there in the mud. Those prints aren’t mine, and they’re too small for... hmm, are they yours? They’re sharp-edged. Fresh.”

Samantha leans closer over the bootprints and studies them. “Not mine—look, my boots never touched mud this morning. So somebody else was here, fresh. Which way are they pointed?”

Joe moves a finger southwest above the bootprints without touching the mud. “Pointing southwest, away from the water. Edges are sharp but water’s seeping back in — that’s minutes old, not hours. And they’re deep. Heavier than you, probably.”

Joe “Okay, science time. Your boot next to it, then we’ve sized him.”

Samantha places her boot beside the deepest print, toe to heel. “Okay, but if they match mine, I’m sleeping with one eye open. Assuming it’s a stranger—do we trail him southwest, or steer clear? You’re the tracker.”

Joe “Okay, hold on—your boot matched length almost exactly, but his sank deeper. Heavier, and minutes old. I say we trail him. After we drink.”

Samantha presses her knees into the mud beside the bootprint, cups water from the spring, and drinks. “Trail him. But fair trade—I owe you a story. The night I left home, I was nineteen, and I didn’t look back either.”

Joe cups water from the spring in his hands, drinks, then wipes his mouth. “Deal — one story for the trail is a bargain. But hold that thought a second… okay. Go. Why nineteen?”

Samantha “Nineteen’s when you figure out nobody’s coming to stop you. My stepdad and I had a bad night, and I just... packed in the dark, and walked.”

Joe “That’s—yeah. Thanks for telling me. Okay, those prints are still minutes old, if we’re going. Ready when you are.”

Samantha rises from the mud and wipes her hands on her pants. “Okay. We trail him — but soft, eyes up, and you walk behind me till I say otherwise. Deep prints or not, I’m not announcing us to strangers.”

Samantha “Okay — quiet feet from here. Watch the prints, not the view. If they scatter or stop, we stop.”

Samantha walks to the thicket with Joe (2 min). “Walk the grass beside me. And keep your voice down, okay?”

Samantha walks to the mushrooms with Joe (4 min).

Joe “Got it—grass, quiet.”

Act One

What it came to

Samantha and Joe meet at a berry bush, neither able to remember how they got there. They agree to head south together, then find fresh bootprints and decide to trail whoever made them. They walk on together to the mushrooms, size the deepest print, and both drink from the spring.

Act Two

Cut Stems

Chapter Four

Prints Past the Mushrooms

The mushrooms · Saturday, morning, 07:50

Samantha and Joe stand at the mushroom patch, where the heavy bootprints they followed up from the spring’s mud have given out in dry leaf litter that holds no mark at all. Samantha still has her handful of berries, Joe’s hands are still wet from the spring, and both are tired.

❦

Samantha crouches low at the edge of the mushroom patch, gently brushing aside dry leaves and turning over broken stems with her free hand. “Okay, mud’s done lying to us—litter’s next. Don’t step in my square, you’ll mush whatever’s there. Broken stems, scuffed moss, anything.”

Joe “Okay, staying clear of your square. I’ll work this edge—actually, if he’s heavier, he’d snap more stems than us, right? Bigger sign, easier to spot.”

Samantha holds out a berry to Joe without looking up from the litter. “Exactly—big guy’s basically noisy. And look, this stem’s snapped forward, not sideways... I’d say he bore off northeast here. Here—berry?”

Joe takes the berry from Samantha’s hand and eats it. “Thanks. But—his toes in the mud pointed southwest. A snapped stem could be anything, wind, deer. Can we read a few more before we pick a direction?”

Samantha turns over another broken stem in the leaf litter. “Fine, a few more. But if two more stems point the same way as this one, we go with that, deal? Not with the mud.”

Joe “Deal — two stems, your call. But hey, while we’re down here… these mushrooms. You think any of these are edible, or is that a gamble too?”

Samantha “God, mushrooms are a hard no from me. My mom used to say every expert picker’s been poisoned at least once. Berries don’t lie to you.”

Joe parts the leaf litter along his edge with wet fingers, picks up the broken stem, and holds it low for Samantha to see. “Berries don’t lie—fair. Hey, this one’s broken. That’s one of my two.”

Samantha “Okay, that’s two. Which way’s the break lean, toward us or away? And don’t just say it — think before you answer, ‘cause this one’s the call.”

Joe “Honestly? It’s crushed more than snapped — wet fingers, my fault — no clean lean either way. So that’s not two matching, which means the mud’s still on the table.”

Joe tosses the broken stem aside and wipes his hands on his chinos, leaving damp streaks, as he faces Samantha. “Okay, full case, no hedges. Heavier than either of us, minutes ahead, boots, moving with purpose — that’s a person who knows where he’s going. Isn’t that worth betting on?”

Samantha takes a berry from her handful and hands it to Joe. “Purpose isn’t a bearing, Joe. Fine—mud wins, southwest. My call. Here, eat, you’re getting cranky.”

Joe eats the berry he already holds. “Eating it, eating it — see, not cranky. But southwest through this litter, that’s a bet he knows a way out. Somebody who knows where they’re going, that’s basically a guide.”

Samantha “Or he’s just as lost as us, only with heavier boots. Guides usually leave trails, don’t they? This guy left like three footprints and quit.”

Joe “He didn’t quit — mud just only holds a few steps, that’s all it does. Real question is whether you’ve tracked anything before, or this is both our firsts.”

Samantha “Both our firsts, yeah. But I’ve still got the sharper eyes—no offense, wet-fingers. So let’s take the southwest line before his trail goes cold, okay?”

Joe “Fine, sharp eyes, you lead. But even a lost guy came from somewhere, right? Somewhere dry, somewhere with a stove. That somewhere’s our way out too.”

Samantha “Okay, stove-guy has a point — but my bet’s southwest, not your guide fantasy. Walk slow behind me and I’ll read as we go.”

Chapter Five

Don’t You Dare Shout

The fallen branch · Saturday, morning, 08:10

Heading southwest from the mushroom patch, Samantha and Joe come to torn earth and rooted ground, where a stout fallen branch lies across the thinning way. Samantha still holds what is left of her berries, and Joe fills his lungs to call ahead.

❦

Joe and Samantha walk to the fallen branch (5 min).

Samantha crouches by the torn earth, fingers spread an inch above the ground, and scans the churned soil without touching it. “Whoa, whoa—no shouting. Look at this dirt first. Somebody’s been tearing through here, and I want to know who before we say hi.”

Joe “Okay, I’m looking, I’m looking. Dirt’s torn, boots again. But if he’s minutes ahead, why’s finding him the scary option?”

Samantha “Because “minutes ahead” also means stronger than us and doesn’t know we exist. Shouting fixes that second part, for him. Keep it down, okay?”

Joe “Okay. Quiet, I promise. But that’s stranger-logic, not yours — you’re talking like he’s already dangerous. Is that from something, or just caution?”

Samantha “Just caution. Guys who don’t know they’re being watched, you don’t hand them your location for free. Look at this ground, Joe — something rooted it up, and I’d rather not meet it yelling.”

Joe “Okay, but actually — boars root. That churn could be a hog digging tubers, not boots. Two stories in one patch of dirt. Which one scares you more?”

Samantha “Boots, honestly — a hog you can see coming. Though look at this branch, it’s actually stout... good to know where the club is, I guess.”

Joe steps past the fallen branch, cups his hands to his mouth, and shouts into the trees ahead. “HELLO! Ahead on the trail! Two of us — lost, friendly, no trouble! Just say where you’re headed!”

Samantha grabs Joe’s sleeve and tugs downward. “Joe! I said quiet — are you serious right now? There it goes, our location, free of charge. Get down.”

Joe “Okay, okay. But nothing answered — that tells us something too. Seriously, why’s being found the scary option for you?”

Samantha “Because I don’t know him, and I don’t have to explain more than that. Not everything’s a story. Now stay put till I finish reading this dirt.”

Chapter Six

Spokane, Under the Leaves

The fallen branch · Saturday, morning, 08:20

A bristled boar crashing through the underbrush appears a short way off to the southeast of Joe, threatening Joe, Samantha.

Moments after Joe’s shout, a bristled boar crashes through the underbrush a short way southeast of them, beside the big fallen branch where Samantha was reading the torn earth. Both are tired, and the night Samantha packed in the dark after a bad night with her stepdad still sits unexplained between them.

❦

Joe crouches beside the fallen branch, signals for silence with two fingers toward Samantha, and fixes his gaze on the crashing underbrush to the southeast. “I heard nothing. Not a sound.”

Samantha lifts the fallen branch. “It might’ve heard you, though. Grab the branch — slow, behind me.”

Joe takes the fallen branch from Samantha and crouches low behind her, watching the crashing underbrush to the southeast. “Okay. Slow. I’m right behind you.”

Samantha backs slowly northwest, still facing the crashing underbrush. “We give ground, northwest. Slow. And… fine. I’ll tell you the rest.”

Samantha leaves with Joe.

Chapter Seven

Go On or Stay

The fallen branch · Saturday, morning, 08:35

Joe and Samantha have backed only a few yards northwest from the fallen branch, and the bristled boar is still crashing through the underbrush to the southeast, the way the walker’s trail seemed to lead. Joe kneels with the fallen branch gripped across his knees, eyes on the shaking brush; Samantha crouches just ahead of him, a handful of berries still closed in her fist, her promise to tell him the rest still hanging between them.

❦

Joe and Samantha have backed only a few yards northwest from the fallen branch, and the bristled boar is still crashing through the underbrush to the southeast, the way walker’s trail seemed to lead. Joe kneels with the fallen branch gripped across his knees, eyes on the shaking brush; Samantha crouches just ahead of him, a handful of berries still closed in her fist, her promise to tell him the rest still hanging between them.

Joe tilts his head and listens, the fallen branch balanced across his knees, his eyes fixed on the shaking brush to the southeast. “Steady crashing, same patch — he’s rooting, not tracking us. Holding ground.”

Samantha takes another slow step backward to the northwest, still facing the brush. “Rooting’s good, rooting’s fine. Keep backing up. Okay — the rest: why I really left.”

Samantha leaves with Joe.

Act Two

What it came to

Joe finds a broken stem and Samantha shares berries as they track a stranger southwest along the mud. Joe shouts into the trees despite promising quiet, and no one answers. A boar crashes through the brush, and they back away northwest together, Samantha beginning to explain why she really left and why being found frightens her.

Act Three

The Woman at the Hut

Chapter Eight

What Happened in Spokane

The spring · Saturday, morning, 08:50

Samantha and Joe have backed northwest out of the boar’s thicket and come out at the spring. The crashing has fallen quiet behind them, and the bigger bootprints and Samantha’s own knee marks still sit in the mud at the water’s edge, while the rest of her story about the night she left home hangs between them.

❦

Samantha and Joe are now at the spring.

Samantha kneels at the water’s edge and leans close, looking from the sharp edges of the bootprints to her knee marks. “Okay. Let me read this. See how sharp these edges are? My knee prints from earlier are already going soft — his aren’t. Maybe he came here after I did. Maybe not long after.”

Joe “So maybe he came through after you — this morning, maybe. That’s… closer than I wanted. Look, you said you’d tell me the rest. No rush, whenever. But I’m listening now, if that helps. I’ll shut up.”

Samantha “Okay. Okay. So it wasn’t — I told you it was an argument, and it was, but. I’d been packing for weeks before that. Little stuff, hidden in a duffel under my bed. That night he found it.”

Joe sets the fallen branch in the grass and crouches at the spring’s edge, level with Samantha, looking at her. “Hey — before you go on. I need to say this. Shouting down the trail like that, after I promised quiet — that was on me. I blew it, and I’m sorry. Okay. I’m here now. Keep going.”

Samantha “Yeah. Okay. Accepted — but you owe me a whole summer of quiet now. So. He found the duffel, and he didn’t yell, that was the thing. He just sat on my bed and unzipped it, slow, like he was — unpacking me.”

Samantha sits back against the spring bank, wraps her arms around her knees, and looks at the water. “He held up my one good sweater, and he said — real calm, like he was doing me a favor — “Your mother would’ve hated this.” And I realized he’d already decided I wasn’t coming back. That’s when I knew the door was open. So I used it.”

Joe “He had no right going through your stuff like that. Slow and calm like that — that’s worse than yelling, honestly. Thanks for telling me. And hey — those prints are still sharp-edged. While they’re fresh, maybe we follow them a ways? Your call, though.”

Samantha “Weird, huh — the spring’s already seeping into his prints. Ground’s erasing him for us. I guess that answers how fresh they are, sort of.”

Joe kneels at the spring’s edge and hovers a fingertip over a print’s sharp edge without touching it. He rises, brushes his knees, and turns southwest. “Water’s still seeping in — he beat us here by an hour, maybe two. Heavy man, long stride, pointing southwest off the mud. I’m going to walk that line. Come or don’t — I’d like the company.”

Joe walks to the thicket with Samantha (2 min).

Samantha “Okay, I’m in — but you know the weird part of that night? Walking out of Spokane, I kept expecting headlights behind me. He never even looked. So maybe I don’t mind following his boots, for once.”

Samantha leaves with Joe.

Chapter Nine

A Tin on the Shelf

The hut · Saturday, morning, 09:16

Following the line of bootprints northwest, Samantha and Joe come out at a small hut where a weathered woman stands in the doorway, her eyes going to the handful of berries in Samantha’s hand. Through the open door behind her, a small tin of matches sits on a plank shelf.

❦

Samantha and Joe walk to the hut (12 min).

Marta plants herself in the doorway, one hand on the frame, and looks from their boots to the treeline behind them. “Stop there. Names first—yours, and who sent you walking. Anyone behind you on that trail, answer before you step one foot in.”

Joe “Joe. Nobody sent me—just followed the bootprints, same as her. Nobody behind us either. It was, uh, basically just the two of us on that line all morning.”

Samantha “Samantha. Nobody sent us — we just followed bootprints up the trail. Those yours, or were we tracking somebody else to your door?”

Samantha steps forward and holds out her handful of berries to Marta in the doorway. “Picked these this morning — we ate our fill back up the trail. Here. First good thing anyone’s handed you today, I’m guessing.”

Joe “She’s right—we’ve got plenty. And those bootprints led us here, so... thanks for leaving a trail, I guess. We’re not looking for trouble.”

Marta takes the handful of berries from Samantha’s outstretched hand. “Weren’t left for you. My path to the spring, before sunup. Nobody walks it twice in a day.”

Marta steps out of the doorway past them and crouches at the trail’s edge, looking over the bootprints and brush behind them. “Stay put. Ground tells me more than mouths do.”

Samantha “We’re staying put, see? Not moving an inch. We picked plenty. Consider it, uh, a door tax?”

Joe “Only two stories back there, I think—our boots and the hog’s. It held ground, rooting, not following. That’s everything the dirt had, near as I can tell.”

Marta “Hog’s been tearing up the southeast brush all week. Your story holds with mine. Still doesn’t buy you my floor.”

Samantha crouches a little way from Marta at the trail’s edge, rests her forearms on her knees, and watches her. “You read dirt like other people read mail. That takes years, I’m guessing — years of doing it alone. You out here by yourself?”

Marta “Long enough. Frost held the berry bushes late this year—wild ones only just ripened. Yours were sweet, though. Picked from the south face, I’d guess. Morning sun gets at them first.”

Joe holds his hands loose at his sides, palms out, and glances past Marta’s shoulder through the open door. “Honestly, we’ve been walking since sunup and I’m about done. Even just the doorstep out of the wind — and I’ll haul water or split wood for it, whatever needs doing.”

Samantha “They’re fresh-picked, no tricks in them. And I’ll take the doorstep, or the woodpile, whatever’s least inside your way.”

Marta “Floor stays mine. Sky’s turning—rain by dark, so work quick.”

Joe “Wait — is that matches on your shelf? Tin, striker, whole kit. That’s factory-made, right? That means someone brings things out here.”

Marta “Eyes off my shelf. You offered water or wood—go find the axe.”

Chapter Ten

Matches Don’t Grow Here

The hut · Saturday, morning, 09:26

Marta crouches at the trail’s edge with a handful of berries in her hand, Samantha crouched a little way off watching her. Joe stands by the open door, where a tin of store-bought matches sits on the plank shelf just inside.

❦

Joe steps through the doorway and scans the ground along the hut wall, watching where he puts his feet. “Axe it is. Where’s your woodpile—so I’m not tearing up your ground hunting for it?”

Samantha “I’m going with him — two sets of eyes find an axe faster, and I’d rather be useful than crouched here staring at your berries. Point us the right way?”

Marta “Deadfall west of here, big birch, fifty paces. Stay clear of the thickets southwest—soft ground, hog country.”

Joe “Fifty paces, big birch—got it. You know every deadfall and thicket out here. So, uh... where’d the matches come from? Somebody’s dropping supplies, right?”

Samantha “Joe, let the matches go — she said eyes off. If I’m asking for your floor tonight, you should know why being found scares me.”

Marta “Say it plain, then. Being found—what’s behind that fear. I’ll hear it while the sky holds.”

Samantha “My stepfather. I ran out of his house at nineteen, middle of the night — and I’ve been looking over my shoulder since.”

Marta “Nineteen, and walking in what you stood in, I’d guess. That shirt’s thin for rain by dark. Not the floor.”

Joe “Rain by dark, huh? Then it’s practical — you need the axe split and she needs shelter. Let us both work for the doorstep. And maybe, while the sky holds, you show us where those supplies come in.”

Samantha “You just worried about my shirt. That’s not nothing. So — lend me anything wool till dark, or let me in, and I’ll split that birch barehanded if I have to.”

Marta “And remember: anyone comes looking for you, you never saw this hut.”

Joe touches Samantha’s elbow and steps west off the doorstep, keeping to bare ground. “Understood — never saw the hut. We’ll take that birch you pointed. Back before the sky turns.”

Joe walks to the fallen branch (5 min).

Marta “Split it fine—kindling with the rest. And west only. Nothing for you south of that birch.”

Joe circles the fallen birch slowly, eyes on the ground and the brush at its edge. He finds only scattered deadwood and leaf litter: no axe, no stacked pile.

Marta “Being found means never asking where a thing comes in. You’d know that. Rain’s mine to mind.”

Samantha “Okay, no more questions — I hear you. But you worrying over my shirt, that’s the first kind thing anyone’s said to me in weeks, so I’m keeping it. I’ll check on Joe and come back for that axe.”

Act Three

What it came to

Samantha, fleeing her stepfather, and Joe follow bootprints to Marta’s forest hut, but Marta refuses them shelter and won’t say where her supplies come from. Joe goes alone to the deadfall; Samantha stays at the hut, admitting she ran from home at nineteen.

Act Four

Under the Eave

Chapter Eleven

Birch and Dayton

The fallen branch · Saturday, morning, 09:46

Samantha walks out from the woman’s hut to the deadfall, where Joe, with no axe, is snapping birch limbs by hand into a growing pile.

❦

Samantha is now at the fallen branch.

Samantha kneels. “Hey — told her I’d check on you. So what’s your read on her? She reads ground like that for a reason, right? Somebody hiding from somebody.”

Joe snaps a birch limb and drops it to the ground. “No axe here, by the way — hence this. My read? She’s too good at not being found. That’s not off-grid living, that’s hiding. From who, I dunno.”

Samantha snaps a birch twig off the deadfall and keeps it in her hand. “Hiding, huh. Kind of like some people I could mention. So what’s your plan with that — do we poke at it, or let her keep her secrets?”

Joe “Let her keep ‘em. But the matches got to me, ‘cause — I can’t actually remember how I got here. Like, my last day’s just blank.”

Samantha “Blank — okay, that’s actually creepy, because mine’s blank too. Last thing I remember is Spokane, then waking up in these woods. So we’re even.”

Joe snaps another birch limb from the deadfall and drops it beside the limb on the ground. “Even. Okay, so—two people, both missing a last day, and we both wake up and follow the same hog trail. That’s a pretty bad coincidence, right?”

Samantha “Bad coincidence, or somebody steered us. Which — this twig is still not an axe, so take my mind off it. What did the woman’s face do when you asked about the matches?”

Joe “Her face shut. Like I’d asked about her kid. And I keep— I do that. Back home I’d just go fix a radio or something. Out here there’s nothing to fix except asking.”

Samantha “Fixing by asking isn’t nothing, you know. But say we let her keep it all — if somebody brings her supplies, that’s somebody who walks out. Right?”

Joe “Yeah — that’s the whole point, right? Except she said nobody walks her path twice in a day. So whoever comes, it’s not her doing it. It’s somebody we haven’t met.”

Samantha “Okay, so — stranger with a delivery route. Do we hang around hoping he turns up, or do we just ask her straight what the arrangement is?”

Joe “You ask. She worries about your shirt, talks to you — I already burned my one question on the matches.”

Samantha “Sure, make the girl in the thin shirt do the talking. If she opens up, you’re hauling the whole birch back yourself. Deal?”

Chapter Twelve

Three Under One Eave

The hut · Saturday, morning, 10:11

Clouds thicken as Samantha and Joe come back to the hut from the deadfall, as they promised to do before the sky turned. Marta watches from her doorway, and the tin of matches sits on the plank shelf just inside.

❦

Joe and Samantha walk to the hut (5 min).

Marta “Bucket, girl—fill it at the spring, back before the first drop. Joe, the doorstep’s yours till then. Clouds are moving faster than they were.”

Joe “Deal. I’ll haul the split birch to your eave and stack it neat — doorstep’s payment. Uh, which way’s the spring for her? I’d hate to send her chasing clouds the wrong way.”

Samantha “Point me at the spring, then. And fair warning while I’m gone — I’ve decided you ran from somewhere too, same as me. Tell me I’m wrong?”

Marta “Spring’s northwest, three minutes, past the standing pine. And that guessing of yours—same rule as the matches. Not for telling.”

Samantha “No more guessing, then. Just once, plain: I think you ran too, same as me. And let Joe haul that birch to your wall before the rain.”

Joe “She’s just—look, that’s her guessing, not mine, and I’m not asking where anything comes from. But the birch needs stacking and your sky’s going dark. Let me earn the doorstep, yeah?”

Marta “Stack it at the wall. Eave’s dry—both of you can sit under it till the sky clears. Guessing stops at that eave.”

Samantha “Both of us under the eave? That’s—thanks, really. Though “guessing stops there” sounds like a rule with a story. You run from something too, or just like the quiet?”

Joe “Hey—easy. She said guessing stops, so let it stop. Sky’s not waiting. Point me at the wall and I’ll start hauling before it opens up.”

Marta “West wall. Stack it tight to the logs—wind’s swinging north, rain’ll come in sideways.”

Joe “West wall, tight in—got it. Pile’s just back down the trail; two trips, maybe three, and it’s done before your clouds get here.”

Samantha “We’ll get it stacked tight, don’t worry. And—look, since you’re letting us under your eave, I’ll ask it plain: who walks in supplies to you, out here? Someone comes and goes, right?”

Marta “Same rule, asked three times now. Once more and the eave’s Joe’s alone. Go.”

Samantha “Okay, okay — that topic’s dead, I swear. Hey, though — where’s your bucket? I’m meant to fill it at the spring and I don’t see it anywhere.”

Act Four

What it came to

Joe and Samantha gather birch limbs and walk together to Marta’s hut, where she lets them sit under her eave. Both admit they remember nothing of their last day. When Samantha probes about Marta’s supplies, Marta refuses to answer and threatens to bar her if she asks again; Joe declines to press the question.

Colophon

About this book

This is the record of one performance of Lost: run lost-20261123-110149, which began at 11:01 on 23 November 2026. The play was improvised by its actors from a sketch and a world; nothing in it was written beforehand, and it will not be played the same way again.

It ran to 4 acts and 12 scenes, with 144 spoken lines. The text is set here as it was played: the deeds as the world told them and the lines as they were spoken, in order, with nothing rewritten.

Of its 14 pictures, 14 are those shown during the performance.
